blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Trace the effects of fiscal policy onto each macroeconomic aim, including the balance of payments and the distribution of income, and weigh where the aims pull against one another.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Onto employment, growth and prices
blocks.text: Where there is spare capacity, an expansionary stance tends to raise output and employment: hired workers spend, and their spending sustains further jobs, so the growth and employment aims move together. As the economy nears full capacity, the same measures tend instead to push the general price level up, so a stance that lowers unemployment adds pressure to prices - the aims begin to move against one another, and the stance cannot serve both at once.

blocks.heading: For whom the effects land
blocks.text: The effects land unevenly. Workers gain as jobs return; firms gain sales where spending rises; savers and households on fixed incomes lose where prices climb, since the same money buys less; and the government's own accounts move with the stance, a tax cut lowering the revenue that funds the very services the aims are pursued through. Naming the party each effect lands on is what turns a stance into an analysis.

blocks.heading: Fiscal policy and the balance of payments
blocks.text: Fiscal policy reaches the balance of payments through spending on imports. A contractionary stance - higher income tax, or cuts in government spending - lowers households' disposable income, so they buy less of everything, imports included. For Namibia, which imports most of its vehicles, fuel and machinery and many of its foods, a large part of any change in spending falls on imports, so a contractionary budget tends to narrow a current account deficit. The cost lands at home: lower spending also means fewer sales for local firms, slower growth and fewer jobs - the conflict between aims set out in topic 4.2. An expansionary stance works the other way: where much of the extra income is spent on imported goods, the current account deficit tends to widen. Fiscal policy can also act on what the country produces over time: government spending on roads, ports and training may lower exporters' costs and raise the quality of what they sell, and a lower company tax may attract foreign firms that produce for export, which tends to strengthen the current account in the longer run, though such effects are slow and uncertain. Greece in the early 2010s is an example from outside Africa: deep cuts in government spending and higher taxes narrowed its large current account deficit, largely because imports fell, while unemployment rose steeply.

blocks.heading: Fiscal policy and the redistribution of income
blocks.text: Fiscal policy is a government's main tool for redistributing income, and it works on both sides of the budget. On the revenue side, a progressive income tax takes a larger share of high incomes than of low ones, so incomes after tax are less unequal than incomes before it. On the spending side, transfers such as the old-age pension and child grants add to the incomes of poorer households, and free or subsidised services such as schools and clinics are worth most, as a share of income, to households with the least. Raising regressive taxes works the other way: a higher value-added tax takes a larger share of a poor household's income, which is why Namibia charges no value-added tax on a list of basic foods such as maize meal and bread. Work invented monthly incomes through: N$3 000 and N$40 000, a gap of N$37 000. A new grant of N$1 400 raises the first to N$4 400; a tax rise of N$1 000 on the second lowers it to N$39 000; the gap narrows to N$34 600. There are limits. Taxes raised steeply on high earners may weaken their incentive to work, invest or start firms, and some may move income out of the country, so the revenue that funds the transfers may fall short of the plan. Whether fiscal policy narrows the gap therefore depends on how progressive the taxes are, how well transfers reach the poorest households, and how strongly high earners respond.

blocks.heading: Borrowing and the future
blocks.text: A deficit-financed programme shifts part of today's cost onto future taxpayers, who meet the interest and repayments from later budgets. Whether that is justified turns on what the borrowed funds buy: a water scheme that raises the district's productive capacity goes some way to repaying itself, a recurring wage bill does not - and on the size of the gap. An invented Vietnamese province that borrowed to build flood defences left later budgets with repayments but left its farms standing; the trade is the same one a Namibian finance minister weighs over an N$8 billion gap.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The aims themselves, and their conflicts, are set out in topic 4.2; the interest-rate route to the same aims is topic 4.4.
